Points of sail: how a yacht sails close to the wind · Ocean Way
A yacht cannot sail straight into the wind, but it can sail at almost any other angle. Here are the points of sail, how to trim for each, and how tacking differs from gybing.
Ocean Way instructors
Updated 1 Nov 2026
The wind and the no-go zone
The points of sail
Heading up and bearing away
Tacking and gybing
True and apparent wind
Reading the telltales
Practise it on the water
No sail works within about 45° of the wind: this is the no-go zone.
As you head up, sheet in; as you bear away, ease out.
Tacking turns the bow through the wind; gybing turns the stern, and the boom swings right across.
Telltales show the airflow: trim or steer until both stream back.
Where the wind comes from

Everything on a sailing yacht starts with the wind direction. Before you touch a sheet (a line that controls a sail), find where the wind is coming from. Feel it on your face and ears, look at the wind indicator at the top of the mast, and watch the ripples on the water.

A sail cannot drive a yacht straight into the wind. There is a sector, roughly 45° either side of the wind, where the sails simply flap and the boat slows down. This is the no-go zone. The exact angle varies with the boat and the sea: a modern cruising yacht in flat water may point a little higher, while a heavy boat in a short chop will not sail as close. If you turn into the no-go zone and stop, you are "in irons": stuck head to wind with no steering.
Every other direction is open to you. The names for the angles between your course and the wind are the points of sail.
No-go zone
Close-hauled
Close reach
Beam reach
Broad reach
Running
Wind

Starboard tack

Points of sail with the wind from the top. No yacht can sail inside the no-go zone, about 45° either side of the wind; boats on the right have the wind over their port side (port tack), the faint ones on the left are on starboard tack.

Each point of sail describes the angle between the bow (the front of the boat) and the wind. The side the wind comes over matters too: with the wind on the starboard (right) side you are on starboard tack, and with it on the port (left) side you are on port tack. The names below apply on either tack.

About 45° to the wind, just outside the no-go zone. Both sails are pulled in tight, close to the centreline of the boat. The yacht heels (leans over) most on this point, the motion is livelier and spray may come over the bow. You steer with small movements, keeping the sails just full.
Around 60° to the wind. Ease (let out) the sheets a little from close-hauled. The boat heels less and usually speeds up.
The wind is at 90°, straight across the side of the boat. The sails are eased about halfway out. For most cruising yachts this is a fast and comfortable point of sail, and a good one to learn on.

Around 135°, with the wind coming from behind the beam, over the back quarter of the boat. The sails are well out. The boat sits more upright and the wind feels lighter than it really is. In a swell she may start to roll.

The wind is from directly behind, at about 180°. The mainsail is eased right out, and the headsail (the sail at the front) often hangs limp in its shadow. You can set the headsail out on the opposite side to the mainsail, which is called goose-winging. Running is where an accidental gybe is most likely, so many skippers prefer a broad reach and change direction in steps.

Turning towards the wind is called heading up. Turning away from it is bearing away. Sail trim follows a simple rule: as you head up, sheet in; as you bear away, ease out. Each change of course needs a change of trim.
A reliable test is to ease the sheet until the luff (the front edge of the sail) starts to flutter, then pull it in just until the flutter stops. That is roughly the right setting for your course.

Two faults are common. Sheets pulled in too tight on a reach make the boat heel and slow down, even though the sail looks full and quiet. Sheets eased too far let the sail flap, which costs speed and wears the cloth. On a broad reach or a run, also check that the boom is not pressing against the shrouds (the wires that hold the mast up from the sides).
To change from one tack to the other, you turn either the bow or the stern through the wind.
Tacking

means turning the bow through the wind. You use it to make progress upwind, zigzagging from close-hauled on one tack to close-hauled on the other. The headsail sheet is released on the old side and pulled in on the new side. The boom moves only a short way, because the mainsail is already in tight. The helm (the person steering) calls "Ready about", the crew answers "Ready", and the helm calls "Tacking" or "Lee-oh" as they turn.
Gybing

means turning the stern (the back of the boat) through the wind. You use it when sailing downwind. This time the wind gets behind the mainsail and swings the boom across the whole width of the boat. In a controlled gybe, the helm calls "Ready to gybe", the crew pulls the mainsheet in to bring the boom towards the centre, the helm turns, and the mainsheet is eased out again on the new side.
Watch out

An accidental gybe happens when you steer too far downwind and the wind catches the back of the mainsail. The boom then slams across with no warning. It can seriously injure anyone in its path and damage the rig. On a run, keep your head below the boom's path, keep the wind a little on the side opposite the boom, and rig a preventer (a line holding the boom forward) when the skipper asks for one.

The true wind is what you feel standing still on the quay. Once the boat moves, its own speed creates a breeze, and the two combine into the apparent wind: the wind you feel on deck and the wind the sails actually use. Sailing upwind, the apparent wind feels stronger and comes from further forward than the true wind. Sailing downwind, it feels lighter. This is why a gentle broad reach can turn into a hard beat when you head up. The wind indicator and the telltales always show the apparent wind.

Telltales are short strips of wool or ribbon on both sides of the headsail, a little back from the luff. They show how the air flows over the sail, and they react well before the sail itself starts to flutter.
Both streaming straight back:
the sail is well trimmed. Keep going.
The windward one lifts or spins
(on the side the wind comes from): the sail is too far out for your course. Sheet in, or bear away a little.
The leeward one lifts or spins
(on the side away from the wind): the sail is in too tight. Ease the sheet, or head up a little.

Close-hauled, the sheet is already in tight, so you correct with the helm: bear away when the windward telltale lifts, head up when the leeward one does. On a reach, hold your course and trim the sheet. Many mainsails also have telltales on the leech (the back edge). When they stream back, the mainsail is not pulled in too hard.

On the Introduction to Yachting course you sail every point of sail, taking turns on the helm and on the sheets until trimming by the telltales becomes a habit. You practise tacking and controlled gybes many times in moderate wind before you do them in a stronger breeze.

Sailing knots: six every crew member uses · Ocean Way
Six knots cover almost every job on a cruising yacht, from mooring to reefing. For each one: what it is for, how to tie it, how to check it and the mistake to avoid.
Rope words
Bowline
Clove hitch
Round turn and two half hitches
Cleat hitch
Figure-of-eight stopper
Reef knot
Coiling and handing over
Bowline for a fixed loop; cleat hitch for making fast on a cleat.
Clove hitch for fenders; round turn and two half hitches for a loaded ring or post.
Figure-of-eight stoppers keep sheets from running out through blocks.
A reef knot is for reef points and sail ties only, never for joining loaded lines.
A few rope words
On a yacht, a rope with a job is called a line: sheets control the sails, halyards hoist them. Knot instructions use a few words:
Working end:
the free end you tie with.
Standing part:
the rest of the line, usually the part that takes the load.
Loop and bight:
a loop is where the line crosses itself; a bight is a U-shaped fold that does not cross.
A good knot is quick to tie, holds under load and comes undone afterwards.
What it is for:

a fixed loop at the end of a line that does not slip or tighten. You use it to put a loop in a mooring line to drop over a bollard, to tie a sheet to the clew (back corner) of a headsail, or to make a loop to go round a person.
Make a small loop in the standing part, with the part leading to the working end lying on top.
Pass the working end up through the small loop from underneath.
Take it round behind the standing part.
Bring it back down through the small loop, alongside itself.
Hold the working end and the side of the big loop together, and pull the standing part to tighten.
How to check it:
the working end finishes inside the big loop, a collar wraps round the standing part, and the tail is at least a hand's width long.
Common mistake:

making the first small loop the wrong way round, with the standing part on top. The knot then pulls straight out. A bowline also cannot be untied under load, and it can shake loose on a flogging sheet.
a quick, adjustable hitch (a knot that ties a line to an object). Its everyday job is hanging fenders from the guardrail (the wire round the deck edge), where you can quickly adjust their height.
Pass the working end over the rail and round it.
Cross the end over its own standing part and take a second turn round the rail, beside the first.
Tuck the working end under this second turn, so it comes out between the two turns.
Pull both parts to tighten.
two neat turns side by side, a diagonal cross over the top, and both ends coming out of the middle in opposite directions.
trusting it with a load that keeps working back and forth: it can slip or roll off. For fenders left out for a while, add a half hitch round the standing part.

tying a line to a ring, rail or post that takes a steady load, such as a mooring ring on a harbour wall or the painter (bow line) of the dinghy. You can tie and untie it under strain, because the round turn takes the load.
Take the working end twice round the ring or post, so the line wraps it completely.
Bring the end over the standing part and tuck it through, making a half hitch.
Make a second half hitch the same way, a little further along the standing part.
Slide both hitches up snug against the round turn.
the two half hitches together look like a clove hitch round the standing part, with a decent tail left over.
tying the second half hitch in the opposite direction to the first. It looks similar but is much less secure. Both hitches must go round the same way.
making fast (securing) a line on a cleat, the two-horned fitting on deck and on pontoons. Use it for mooring lines and halyards.
Lead the line to the far horn of the cleat first, the one furthest from where the load comes from.
Take a full turn round the base of the cleat, under both horns.
Cross over the top and round the opposite horn to make a figure of eight. One or two figures of eight are enough.
Finish with a locking hitch: twist a small loop so the line lies under itself, drop it over a horn and pull it tight. The tail should lie parallel with the turn below it.
the crossings are neat and lie on top of each other, and the line leads straight onto the cleat without rubbing on its edge.
piling on extra turns and hitches. A tangle jams under load and cannot be released fast. Some skippers want no locking hitch on sheets for the same reason; follow the skipper's way.

a stopper knot in the end of a line, so it cannot run out through a block (pulley), clutch or fairlead. Tie one in the tail of each headsail sheet, so a sheet let go in a hurry cannot run away forward.
Take the working end over the standing part to make a loop.
Pass it round behind the standing part.
Bring it back down through the loop from the front.
Pull tight, leaving a short tail.
it looks like the figure 8 and is clearly too fat to pass through the block.
tying a simple overhand knot instead. It is smaller, can jam so hard that it has to be cut, and may pull through a large block.
Reef knot, and its limits
tying the two ends of the same line together round something soft. Examples are the reef points (short ties) that gather the bundle of a reefed mainsail, and sail ties.
Take the left end over and under the right.
Take the end that is now on the right over and under the left.
Pull both ends to tighten.
the knot lies flat and symmetrical, and each end lies alongside its own standing part, both on the same side.
crossing the same way twice, which makes a granny knot. It slips or jams.

Never use a reef knot to join two lines that will take a load, especially lines of different thickness. It can capsize (spill into a shape that slides apart) without warning. To join two lines, learn the sheet bend. When reefing, tie reef points round the sail only, not round the boom, so the sail does not tear if the reefing line fails.
Coiling and handing over a line
After you make fast, tidy the tail so it runs free next time.
Coiling:

work from the fixed end towards the free end, making even loops in one hand. Three-strand rope is usually coiled clockwise. Braided rope kinks in round coils, so lay it in figure-of-eight loops or flake it (let it fall loosely so it runs without twisting).
Hanging a halyard tail:
reach through the coil, pull a bight of the line from near the cleat back through it, twist it and hang it over the top horn of the cleat.
Handing over:

tell the person on the quay what you want, for example "Bow line, round the bollard and back to me." Make sure the end on board is made fast, pass or throw the line in a loose coil, and never wrap a loaded line round your hand.

On the Introduction to Yachting course you tie these knots for real jobs: fenders on before entering harbour, sheets on the headsail, lines ashore when you moor. You practise until you can tie each one without looking, as you will need to at night.
Right of way at sea: the rules skippers use daily · Ocean Way
The COLREGs decide who keeps clear when two vessels meet. These are the rules a yacht skipper applies every day, from keeping a lookout to dealing with big ships in a channel.
Lookout and safe speed
Risk of collision
Taking action
Two sailing vessels
Overtaking, head-on, crossing
Give-way and stand-on
Who gives way to whom
Narrow channels
Keep a proper lookout; a steady bearing with a closing range means risk of collision.
Port tack gives way to starboard; windward gives way to leeward; the overtaking vessel always keeps clear.
Give-way vessels act early and boldly; stand-on vessels hold course and speed.
With the engine in gear you are a power-driven vessel, even with sails up.

The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, known as the COLREGs, apply to every vessel, from a cruise ship to a dinghy; some ports add local rules on top. They begin with what everyone must do all the time.
Rule 5, lookout.

Every vessel must keep a proper lookout at all times, by sight and hearing and by every other available means, such as radar and AIS (which shows ships' positions on a screen). On a yacht, check the whole horizon regularly, including behind the headsail.
Rule 6, safe speed.

Every vessel must go at a speed that lets her take proper action to avoid a collision and stop within a suitable distance. There is no fixed number. It depends on visibility, traffic, how quickly your boat stops and turns, wind, sea and current, shore lights at night and the depth under the keel.
Is there a risk of collision?
Rule 7

asks you to decide early whether a risk of collision exists. The simplest test is the compass bearing. Take a bearing of the other vessel with a hand-bearing compass, or line her up with a stanchion (an upright guardrail post) while holding a steady course, then repeat after a minute or two.
If the bearing stays steady and the vessel is getting closer, you are on a collision course.
If the bearing moves clearly ahead or astern, you will probably pass clear.
With large ships, tows or at close range, a risk can exist even when the bearing changes. If in doubt, assume the risk exists. Never decide on a single look or radar reading.
How to take action
Rule 8

says avoiding action must be taken in ample time, be large enough to be obvious to the other vessel by eye or by radar, and leave you passing at a safe distance. Avoid a series of small changes, and keep checking until she is past and clear.

With sea room, a large change of course alone is often best; you can also slow down, stop or go astern (reverse). A clear turn to pass well astern of a ship shows your intention; a nudge of a few degrees does not.
Rule 12
applies when two vessels, both under sail alone, approach each other. With the wind on your port (left) side you are on port tack. The windward side is the side opposite the mainsail.
Wind on different sides:
the vessel on port tack keeps out of the way of the one on starboard tack.
Wind on the same side:
the windward vessel (the one further upwind) keeps out of the way of the leeward one.
Cannot tell:
on port tack, if you see a vessel to windward and cannot tell her tack, keep out of the way.
Overtaking, head-on and crossing
Rule 13, overtaking.

Any vessel overtaking another keeps out of the way, whatever type either vessel is. This overrides Rules 12 and 18: a sailing yacht overtaking a motor boat keeps clear of it. You are overtaking if you approach from more than 22.5° abaft her beam (behind the line across her middle), where at night you would see only her stern light. If in doubt, assume you are overtaking.
Rule 14, head-on.
When two power-driven vessels meet on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses, each turns to starboard so they pass port side to port side.
Rule 15, crossing.
When two power-driven vessels cross, the one that has the other on her own starboard side gives way and, if she can, avoids crossing ahead. In short: if you see her red port sidelight, you give way.
Give-way and stand-on duties
Rule 16:
the give-way vessel takes early and substantial action to keep well clear, ideally passing astern rather than crossing ahead.
Rule 17:

the stand-on vessel keeps her course and speed. That is a duty, not a privilege: the give-way vessel relies on you being predictable. If she is clearly not taking proper action, sound at least five short, rapid blasts (Rule 34); you
may
also act on your own. If she is so close that her action alone cannot prevent a collision, you
must
act. A power-driven stand-on vessel should then avoid turning to port for a vessel on her own port side. None of this frees the give-way vessel from her duty.
Rule 18

sets the order between different kinds of vessel, except where Rules 9, 10 (traffic separation schemes) and 13 say otherwise. Broadly, the less able a vessel is to manoeuvre, the more others keep clear of her.

A power-driven vessel keeps out of the way of a vessel not under command (unable to manoeuvre, for example after a breakdown), a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (such as a dredger at work), a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel.
A sailing vessel keeps out of the way of the first three.
Where possible, every vessel avoids impeding a vessel constrained by her draught (a deep ship limited to the deep water).

"Engaged in fishing" means with nets, lines or trawls that restrict her movement; a boat trolling a line does not count. A sailing vessel is one under sail with any engine not in use. Once the engine drives the propeller, a sailing yacht is a power-driven vessel, even with every sail set.

A motorsailing yacht follows the rules for a power-driven vessel, so she gives way to sailing yachts. By day she shows a cone, point down, forward where it can best be seen. At night she shows a steaming light (a white masthead light) with her sidelights and stern light, never the tricolour at the masthead. Others judge you by what they see: without the cone, a motorsailing yacht looks like a sailing vessel standing on.

Narrow channels and big ships
Rule 9

covers narrow channels and fairways, such as a buoyed harbour approach. Keep as near to the outer edge of the channel on your starboard side as is safe and practicable. A vessel under 20 metres long, or any sailing vessel, must not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only inside the channel. Do not cross a channel if that would impede such a vessel, and avoid anchoring in it.

"Must not impede" means acting early, before any risk of collision develops. A large ship may need well over a mile to stop, and from her bridge a yacht close ahead can be hidden under the bow. Near busy ferry ports such as Piraeus or Bodrum, assume the ship has not seen you. If you must cross, cross quickly and at right angles. If a ship sounds five or more short blasts, she doubts you are keeping clear: act at once.

On the International Bareboat Skipper course, each time another vessel appears you take bearings, decide who gives way and say it aloud before you act. You also practise identifying vessels by their lights and shapes.

Navigation lights and day shapes explained · Ocean Way
At night, lights are how you know what another vessel is, which way she is heading and who keeps clear. This guide covers the lights a yacht shows and the ones you will meet.
How the lights work
Under sail
Under engine
At anchor and day shapes
Common sights at night
Practise it
Each light covers a fixed arc: masthead 225°, sidelights 112.5° each, sternlight 135°.
Under sail: sidelights and sternlight, or a tricolour under 20 m. Under engine: add the masthead light and switch off the tricolour.
At anchor: one all-round white light by night, one black ball by day.
Green over white is a trawler, red over white other fishing, red-white-red a vessel restricted in ability to manoeuvre.

Part C of the COLREGs (the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, Rules 20 to 31) sets out which lights and shapes every vessel must show. Lights are shown from sunset to sunrise and in restricted visibility. Shapes are their daytime equivalent: black balls, cones and diamonds.
Each light shines only over a fixed arc, measured from right ahead. Rule 21 defines them:
Masthead light

: white, shining forward over 225°, from right ahead to 22.5° abaft (behind) the beam on each side. Despite the name, on a yacht it is usually fitted partway up the front of the mast. Sailors often call it the steaming light.
Sidelights
: red on the port (left) side and green on the starboard (right) side, each covering 112.5°, from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam.
Sternlight
: white, shining aft over 135°, 67.5° each side of right astern.
All-round light
: any colour, visible over the full 360°.

The arcs fit together. The sternlight covers exactly the sector the sidelights and masthead light leave dark, so from any direction you see a combination that tells you which way the other vessel is pointing. See only green and you are looking at her starboard side.

Minimum ranges depend on size. For a vessel of 12 to 20 metres the masthead light must be visible at 3 miles and the sidelights and sternlight at 2 miles. Under 12 metres the figures drop to 2 miles for the masthead light and sternlight, and 1 mile for the sidelights. A small yacht's lights are dim. Do not assume a ship has seen you.

A sailing yacht under sail
Under Rule 25, a sailing vessel underway (not at anchor, made fast or aground) shows
sidelights and a sternlight
, and nothing else. No masthead light. The absence of a white light above the sidelights is what tells other vessels you are sailing.
A sailing vessel under 20 metres may instead combine the three into one
tricolour

lantern at or near the top of the mast. It is more visible over waves and uses less power, which is why most cruising yachts have one. You use either the tricolour or the deck-level lights, never both together.

Rule 25 also allows two optional all-round lights at the masthead, red over green, in addition to the deck-level sidelights and sternlight. They are rare on yachts and must not be combined with a tricolour.
Under engine and motorsailing
The moment the engine is in gear and driving the boat, you are a power-driven vessel under the rules, even with the sails up. You lose the sailing vessel's privileges and your lights must change:
Switch on the
masthead light
(steaming light).
Show
sidelights and sternlight
at deck level.
Switch off the tricolour.
It may only be used under sail. A tricolour with a steaming light below it is a common mistake and gives a confusing picture.
By day, a vessel under sail that is also motoring must show a
cone, point down
, forward where it can best be seen (Rule 25(e)). Few yachts bother, but it is required.
At anchor and other day shapes
At anchor, a vessel under 50 metres shows one
all-round white light
where it can best be seen (Rule 30). By day she shows one black
ball

in the forepart. Vessels of 50 metres or more show two anchor lights, the forward one higher. In a crowded Greek or Croatian anchorage, an anchor light at the masthead can be hard to spot from a dinghy or from a boat coming in; many skippers add a light lower down as well.
Other day shapes worth knowing:
Two cones, points together: fishing.
Ball, diamond, ball: restricted in ability to manoeuvre.
Two balls: not under command (unable to manoeuvre, for example after an engine or steering failure).
A diamond: towing, where the tow is over 200 metres long.
Power-driven vessels

A power-driven vessel under 50 metres shows a masthead light, sidelights and a sternlight. From right ahead you see white above red and green. From her starboard side, white and green. From her port side, white and red. From astern, a single white sternlight, which looks the same as a sailing vessel from astern.

A vessel of 50 metres or more must carry a second masthead light, further aft and higher than the first. The pair works like a gunsight. If the two white lights are in a vertical line with both sidelights visible, she is coming straight at you. As they open out, you can read which way she is turning.
Fishing vessels
Fishing vessels show two all-round lights in a vertical line.
Green over white
means trawling (dragging a net).
Red over white

means other fishing, such as nets or long lines. If they are making way through the water, they add sidelights and a sternlight. In the Aegean and along the Turkish coast, expect small fishing boats close inshore at night.
Restricted and towing
A vessel
restricted in ability to manoeuvre
by her work, such as a dredger, cable layer or a ship refuelling at sea, shows
red, white, red
all-round lights in a vertical line, plus normal steaming lights if making way. A vessel
towing

shows two masthead lights in a vertical line (three if the tow is over 200 metres), sidelights, sternlight and a yellow towing light above the sternlight. The tow behind her shows sidelights and a sternlight. Never pass between a tug and its tow.

The "what to do" column is a guide, not a substitute for the steering rules. Rule 18 says a sailing vessel keeps clear of vessels fishing, restricted in ability to manoeuvre and not under command. Whatever the rules say, if the compass bearing of another vessel's lights does not change while the range closes, there is a risk of collision. Act early.

A big ship can be hard to judge at night. Her lights may sit high against shore lights, and she covers a mile in a few minutes. If in doubt, alter course early and by a large amount so the change is obvious, and call on VHF channel 16 if needed.

On our courses you practise this during night passages: identifying real lights from the cockpit, taking bearings on them and deciding who gives way. Before each night sail you also check your own lights and switch between tricolour and steaming light as you change from sail to engine.
